summary: Defines a SIP event package for registrations. Registrations are state in the network that can change, for example when administrators alter them, and this lets a user agent be notified when that state changes. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: If your phone is signed up somewhere, you may want a message when that listing changes. This lets a phone subscribe to news about its own sign-in, so it hears about changes right away.

questions: how to get notified when sip registration changes
what is the sip reg event package
how do i get notified when a sip registration changes
what is an address-of-record in sip
subtitle: A SIP event package that tells subscribers when the registrations for a user change.

tldr.problem: A SIP registration binds a user's address to one or more contacts, and that state can change through refreshes, expiry or administrator action. Nothing let user agents or applications hear about those changes.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the event package named reg for the SIP SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY framework. Notifiers send an XML document (application/reginfo+xml) that lists the contacts bound to an address-of-record and why each one changed.
tldr.outcome: Devices can be told to re-register, presence servers can build on registration state, and applications can react when a user comes online. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 6140.

facts.label: Notification rate
facts.value: No faster than once every 5 seconds (RECOMMENDED)

today: RFC 3680 is a Proposed Standard that has not been obsoleted, but it is updated by RFC 6140.

sections.title: Registrations as Changing State
sections.content:
In the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP), a registration is a binding between a SIP URI called an address-of-record and one or more contact URIs. When a proxy gets a request for the address-of-record, it uses the bound contacts to forward or redirect it.

The REGISTER method lets a user agent add or remove contacts and query the current set. Registrations also change because of administrator policy (a suspected fraud can get a registration deleted) and because they expire if not refreshed. That makes registrations a piece of dynamic network state.

The SIP Events framework defines SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY and the idea of a package, a concrete use of the framework for one class of events. This RFC defines the package for registration state.
sections.plainLanguage: Your phone number is linked to the places where you can be reached, and that list changes. This lets other people sign up to hear about the changes.

sections.title: Usage Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC gives three illustrative uses.

  • Forcing re-authentication. Always-on wireless devices can be compromised. A device subscribes to the registration state of its address-of-record. If an administrator shortens the registration, for example when fraud is suspected, the server notifies the device, which can re-register and re-authenticate. If it cannot, the registration expires soon after.
  • Composing presence. Registration state is raw input to a user's presence document. A presence server separate from the registration server can subscribe to the registration server to learn it.
  • Welcome notices. An application server subscribes to a user's registration. When the user turns on their phone in a foreign country and registers, the application learns of it and sends a SIP MESSAGE with a welcome.
sections.plainLanguage: Three examples: a guard asks you to show your ID again, a map app learns where you can be reached, and a hotel greets you when you arrive.

sections.title: The reg Package Definition
sections.content:
The package name is reg, sent in the Event header of SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY. It defines no package-specific Event header parameters, and state agents play no role.

A SUBSCRIBE MAY carry a body used for filtering, but the format is out of scope. Without a body, the default policy applies: a notification for every change in any contact, containing only the contacts that changed. Notifications triggered by the SUBSCRIBE itself carry full state, the list of all contacts bound to the address-of-record.

The default registration expiration is 3600 seconds, so the default subscription duration is slightly longer at 3761 seconds, which helps avoid coupling of subscription and registration refreshes. Clients MAY ask for a different duration with an Expires header.

Registration state can be sensitive, so subscriptions SHOULD be authenticated and authorized, and it is RECOMMENDED that a user may subscribe to their own registration state. A subscriber MUST NOT create multiple dialogs from one subscription request, since there is no need to fork. Servers are RECOMMENDED not to send notifications to one subscriber more often than once every 5 seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: The sign-up sheet is called reg. By default you get a note about each change, and your sign-up lasts a little over an hour unless you ask for something else.

sections.title: State Machines and When to Notify
sections.content:
To decide when to notify, the RFC models a finite state machine for each address-of-record with the states init, active and terminated. It exists even when no contacts are registered, so a subscriber can learn that there are none. The first contact moves it from init to active. When the last contact expires or is removed it goes to terminated and immediately back to init, and that last transition MUST NOT be reported in a NOTIFY.

Each contact has its own machine, created when the contact is registered and moving to active. Events that keep it active are refreshed and shortened. Events that end the binding are expired, deactivated (the administrator removed it but wants the client to try registering again), probation (re-register later), unregistered (a REGISTER set the expiration to zero) and rejected (re-registering will not help). A contact can also become active through registered (a REGISTER) or created (administrative or other non-SIP means).

Whether a transition triggers a NOTIFY is policy dependent, except for the one that MUST NOT. Notifications SHOULD list only contacts that changed, but a fetch (a SUBSCRIBE with Expires of 0) SHOULD return the full state of all contacts.
sections.plainLanguage: Each phone number goes through three stages: nobody listed yet, someone listed, and no longer listed. The note says which stage it is in and why it changed.

sections.title: The Registration Information Document
sections.content:
Notification bodies use application/reginfo+xml, which every subscriber and notifier MUST support and which is the default when no Accept header is present. The document MUST be well-formed XML 1.0, SHOULD be valid, and MUST be UTF-8. Its namespace is urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:reginfo.

The root reginfo element has a required version that starts at 0 and goes up by one per document within a subscription, and a required state of full or partial. It holds registration elements, each with aor, id and state (init, active or terminated). Each registration holds contact elements with an id, a state (active or terminated) and an event, plus a uri element and optional display-name and unknown-param elements. The expires attribute MUST be present for a shortened event, and retry-after MUST be present for probation. Optional attributes include duration-registered, q, callid and cseq.

A subscriber keeps a table per registration, keyed by id, with a row per contact. If a new version is exactly one higher than the local one it is processed. If it is more than one higher, the subscriber processes it and SHOULD request a refresh to get full state. A lower version is discarded. Full state replaces all tables, while partial state updates them.
sections.plainLanguage: Each note is a form with a version number, a list of people and a list of ways to reach them. If you miss a note, you can see it from the number and ask for a full copy.

sections.title: Example Call Flow
sections.content: The example shows the welcome notice application. An application sends a SUBSCRIBE with Event: reg for a user, and the registrar answers 200 OK and sends a first NOTIFY. Because nobody is registered yet, the registration state is init. Later the user's device sends a REGISTER, the registrar answers 200 OK, and a second NOTIFY goes to the application with a partial document whose contact has the event registered. The application then sends a SIP MESSAGE to the device.
sections.plainLanguage: An app asks to be told when Joe turns on his phone. When he does, the app gets a note and says hello.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The security considerations of the SIP Events framework apply. The RFC adds that registration information is sensitive and potentially private. Subscriptions SHOULD be authenticated and authorized under local policy, and notifications SHOULD be protected for confidentiality, integrity and verification of subscriber identity, for example by using a SIPS URL or protecting the bodies with S/MIME.

IANA registrations cover the event package reg, the MIME type application/reginfo+xml, and the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:reginfo.
sections.plainLanguage: Where someone can be reached is private, so only people who prove who they are and are allowed should be able to ask, and the notes should be sealed.
